mainTopic: Using the money of blemished animals to buy replacement offerings, and which animal is holy when a person consecrates 'one of my animals' without naming it.
overview: The גמרא first explains why the money of one blemished bull ('this bull') may buy two bulls, even though someone who promised 'a bull worth a מנה' may not bring two cheaper ones. It then explains that רבי forbids bringing one bull for two because it is like promising a large animal and bringing a small one. The גמרא shows that רבי really argues on every case in that משנה. A ברייתא about buying two rams with a bull's money shows that the חכמים allow switching species. The גמרא resolves contradictions about this by saying that two תנאים report the views of the חכמים and of רבי differently. רב then limits the rule of buying two bulls: it does not apply if the person said 'this bull and its value are upon me.' A new משנה teaches which animal is holy when someone says 'one of my animals is הקדש.' The גמרא discusses whether 'a bull among my bulls' means the largest, defends that reading against challenges, and ends with a new challenge from a sale of 'a house among my houses' that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Challenge from the earlier rule about a bull worth a מנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the משנה's ruling that two bulls may be brought with the money of one blemished bull. It points to the earlier משנה: one who promised a bull worth a מנה and brought two bulls worth a מנה together has not fulfilled his vow.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: But didn't you say in the earlier clause: if someone said 'a bull worth a מנה' and brought two bulls together worth a מנה, he has not fulfilled his obligation?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the משנה's rule that one blemished bull's money can buy two bulls. It quotes an earlier rule that seems to say two smaller animals cannot replace one bigger animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה says that if 'this bull' became blemished, he may bring two bulls with its money. But the earlier משנה said that someone who promised 'a bull worth a מנה' cannot bring two cheaper bulls worth a מנה in total. The two rules seem to contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion of the משנה begins here
The first or earlier clause; here, the earlier משנה
A sum of money equal to one hundred דינרים
He has not fulfilled his obligation

phrases.english: GEMARA:
But didn't you say in the first clause:
phrases.notes: He means the earlier משנה, on daf 107b.

phrases.english: 'A bull worth a hundred dinars,' and he brought two worth a hundred dinars together,
he has not fulfilled his obligation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא's discussion of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that two bulls may be brought with the money of one blemished bull.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The earlier משנה rules that two bulls cannot replace one promised bull worth a מנה. So how can our משנה allow two bulls in place of one?

steps.title: A specific bull that became blemished is different
steps.stepSummary: The answer: when someone says 'this bull' and it becomes blemished, the case is different from a general promise of 'a bull worth a מנה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he said 'this bull' and it became blemished, it is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that the two cases are not the same.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the earlier משנה, he took on a general obligation of 'a bull worth a מנה', so he must bring exactly that. Here he only set aside one specific bull, and it is now blemished. So he is no longer bound by the exact terms of a promise, and its money may be used for two bulls.

keyTerms.meaning: 'This bull': a promise about one specific animal
Became blemished and unfit to be brought as an offering
It is different

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two kinds of promise. 'A bull' (general) means you owe an animal that matches your words. 'This bull' (specific) means only that animal was owed, so once it is blemished, the rule changes.

phrases.english: 'This bull,' and it became blemished,
is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between cases: a specific animal versus a general promise.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two rules contradict each other, since both involve replacing one bull with two.
steps.terutzMaskana: A general promise ('a bull worth a מנה') must be kept exactly as stated. A specific animal ('this bull') that became blemished frees its money to be used for two bulls.

steps.title: Why does רבי forbid bringing one bull for two?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's case of two specific bulls that became blemished. The first opinion allows bringing one bull with their money, but רבי forbids it. The גמרא asks for רבי's reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'These two bulls are an עולה,' and they became blemished: if he wants, he may bring one bull with their money. But רבי forbids this. What is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next case in the משנה and asks why רבי forbids it. This sets up the explanation in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Based on step 2, you might expect that blemished specific animals free up their money completely. So why should רבי object to bringing just one bull? The גמרא wants to know what bothers him.

keyTerms.meaning: A burnt offering, burned completely on the מזבח
With their money (the money paid to redeem the blemished animals)
Forbids
What is the reason?

phrases.english: 'These two bulls are a burnt offering,' and they became blemished,
if he wishes, he may bring one with their money,
and Rabbi forbids it.
What is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to the next case in the משנה, the reverse situation: two bulls replaced by one.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reasoning behind רבי's ruling that one bull may not be brought with the money of two blemished bulls.

steps.title: It is like promising a big animal and bringing a small one
steps.stepSummary: רבי's reason: bringing one bull instead of two is like promising a large animal and bringing a small one. Even though the original bulls became blemished, רבי does not allow this from the start.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because it is like a case of 'a large one, and he brought a small one.' Even though the bulls became blemished, רבי does not allow it from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains רבי's reasoning: one bull is less than the two he set aside, just as a small animal is less than a big one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier משנה says that someone who promised a large animal and brought a small one has not fulfilled his vow. רבי treats one bull in place of two the same way. He admits the blemish makes the case weaker, but he still will not allow it לכתחילה (from the start).

keyTerms.meaning: He promised a large animal and brought a small one
Even though
From the start; as the proper way to act in the first place

steps.whatToRemember: One blemished specific bull may be replaced by two (step 2). But for two blemished bulls replaced by one, רבי forbids it לכתחילה, because it is like promising a big animal and bringing a small one.

phrases.english: Because it is like
'a large one, and he brought a small one,'
and even though it became blemished,
Rabbi does not permit it from the start.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּהָוֵה לֵיהּ גָּדוֹל וְהֵבִיא קָטָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Replacing two bulls with one is like promising a large animal and bringing a small one. So even after the bulls became blemished, רבי does not allow it לכתחילה.

steps.title: Why doesn't רבי also argue on the first case?
steps.stepSummary: If רבי's reason is 'large and small,' he should also argue on the first case of the משנה, where two bulls are brought with the money of one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let רבי also disagree in the first part of the משנה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי's reason from Step 4. If it is true, רבי should also argue on the first case of the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי said that bringing one bull instead of two is like promising a big animal and bringing a small one. In the first case of the משנה, someone brings two bulls with the money of one, which is like promising a small animal and bringing a big one. The same logic should make רבי forbid that too, yet the משנה shows him arguing only on the later case.

keyTerms.meaning: Let him disagree
The first part (opening clause) of the משנה
Also, too

phrases.english: But let him disagree in the first clause as well!
phrases.notes: The first clause is the case where one bull became blemished and he brings two bulls with its money.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes רבי's reason from Step 4 onto the first case of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The fact that רבי's disagreement appears only in the later case of the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Changing the size of the offering should work in both directions. Two for one is 'small promised, big brought,' so רבי's logic should apply there too.

steps.title: רבי argues on everything, but waited for the חכמים to finish
steps.stepSummary: רבי disagrees with both cases. He simply waited until the חכמים finished their whole statement before voicing his disagreement.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי disagrees with the whole matter. He waited for the חכמים until they finished their words, and then disagreed with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that רבי really does argue on the first case too. His words come only at the end because he let the חכמים finish speaking first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The placement of רבי's opinion at the end of the משנה does not mean it covers only the last case. His disagreement reaches back to every ruling the חכמים made in that section, including two bulls for one.

keyTerms.meaning: On the entire matter
Waited
They finished their words

phrases.english: Rabbi disagrees with the entire matter,
and he waited for the Rabbis
until they completed their statement,
and then he disagreed with them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 5 by reading רבי's disagreement as covering the whole משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the scope of an opinion in the משנה: it applies to all the clauses before it.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since רבי's words come right after the last case, we assumed he argues only there.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי argues on both cases. He simply waited until the חכמים finished their whole statement, and then disagreed.

steps.title: Proof from the ram and the lamb
steps.stepSummary: The משנה about a ram and a lamb shows that רבי forbids switching even to a bigger animal, which proves he argues on the first case too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that this is so, for the משנה teaches: If someone said 'This ram is an עולה' and it became blemished, he may bring a lamb with its money if he wishes. If he said 'This lamb is an עולה' and it became blemished, he may bring a ram with its money if he wishes. And רבי forbids it. Learn from this.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings proof for its answer from another case in the משנה. There רבי forbids switching from a lamb to a ram, even though a ram is the bigger animal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the lamb-to-ram case the person is upgrading, which is like 'small promised, big brought,' and רבי still forbids it. So רבי also forbids bringing two bulls with the money of one. This confirms that he argues on the first case of our משנה too.

keyTerms.meaning: Know (that this is so). Introduces a supporting proof
Became blemished (unfit for the מזבח)
With its money (the redemption money of the blemished animal)
Ram (an older, larger sheep) / lamb (a young sheep)
Forbids
Learn from this. The proof is accepted

steps.whatToRemember: According to the גמרא's conclusion, רבי forbids any change from what was originally designated, whether to something smaller or to something bigger. He argues on every case of the משנה.

phrases.english: Know that this is so, as it teaches:
'This ram is a burnt offering,' and it became blemished:
if he wishes, he may bring a lamb with its money;
'This lamb is for a burnt offering,' and it became blemished:
if he wishes, he may bring a ram with its money,
and Rabbi prohibits it.
Conclude from it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer of Step 6 with evidence from a parallel case.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי also argues on the first case (two bulls brought with the money of one).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה's case of a lamb that became blemished, where the חכמים allow bringing a ram and רבי forbids it.

steps.title: Switching from one species to another
steps.stepSummary: A new question: according to the חכמים, may the money of a blemished animal of one species be used to buy a different species?
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: What is the law about switching from one species to another species?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. The חכמים allow changes within the same species, so what about changing to a completely different species?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, the cases involved one bull versus two bulls, or a ram versus a lamb, which are all within one species (bulls, or sheep). The new question is whether the חכמים would allow a bigger jump, like using the money of a blemished bull to buy rams. This step only asks; the answer comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before them (an open question)
From one species to another species
What (is the law)?

steps.confusionAlert: A ram and a lamb are both sheep, so they count as the same species. 'Species to species' means something like bull to ram.

phrases.english: A dilemma was raised before them:
From one species to another species, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the dispute between רבי and the חכמים to a new question about how far the חכמים' leniency reaches.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether, according to the חכמים, the redemption money of a blemished animal may be used to buy an animal of a different species.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows the חכמים allow switching a bull for rams
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that the money of a blemished bull cannot buy one ram but can buy two rams. רבי forbids this because there is no mixing. So the חכמים allow switching species.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone says 'This bull is an עולה,' and it became blemished, he may not bring one ram with its money, but he may bring two rams with its money. רבי forbids this, because there is no mixing. Learn from this that switching species is allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to answer the question from step 8: can blemished-animal money buy a different kind of animal? The answer from the ברייתא is yes, according to the חכמים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא allows bull money to buy two rams. That means changing species (bull to ram) is fine for the חכמים. רבי disagrees, but only for a separate reason about the flour-and-oil offerings that go with the animals.

keyTerms.meaning: It became blemished (unfit to be offered)
With its money (the money from redeeming the blemished animal)
A ram
Mixing (of the flour and oil of the accompanying meal offering)
Learn from this (the proof is accepted)

phrases.english: Come and hear: 'This bull is a burnt offering,'
and it became blemished – he may not bring a ram with its money,
but he may bring two rams with its money,
and רבי forbids it,
because there is no mixing.
phrases.notes: Each ram needs its own flour-and-oil offering, and these can't be mixed together into one like the single bull's offering.

phrases.english: Learn from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in step 8 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: According to the חכמים, the money of a blemished animal may be used to buy a different species.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: the money of a blemished bull may buy two rams, but not one.

steps.title: Why does the ברייתא need two rams?
steps.stepSummary: If the חכמים allow switching, why do they require two rams? For a blemished animal, the חכמים don't care about large versus small, so one ram should be enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why specifically two rams? Even one ram should be allowed! After all, when the animal became blemished, the חכמים make no difference between a large animal and a small one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ברייתא it just used. It asks why the ברייתא insists on two rams.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From our משנה we know the חכמים allow bringing a smaller animal in place of a blemished larger one (one bull instead of two). So bringing one ram, which is smaller than a bull, should also be fine. Requiring two rams seems to contradict that.

keyTerms.meaning: Why specifically this case? (why mention this detail?)
It makes no difference to them
Large and small (a bigger animal versus a smaller one)

phrases.english: If so, why specifically two?
Even one should be allowed too!
For in a case where it became blemished,
according to the Rabbis it makes no difference to them
whether it is large or small!
phrases.notes: This points back to our משנה, where the חכמים let him bring one bull instead of the two he promised.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges a detail of the ברייתא brought as proof in step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's requirement of two rams, according to the חכמים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The חכמים in our משנה allow a small animal in place of a blemished large one. So one ram should suffice, and the ברייתא's 'two' seems to contradict the משנה.

steps.title: Two תנאים disagree about the view of the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: The answer: two תנאים disagree about what the חכמים hold. One version of the חכמים allows small for large; the other does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are two תנאים, and they disagree about the opinion of the חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 10. The משנה and the ברייתא simply report the view of the חכמים differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the תנא of our משנה, the חכמים allow a smaller animal in place of a blemished larger one. According to the תנא of the ברייתא, the חכמים do not allow that, which is why he needs two rams. Either way, the ברייתא still shows that switching species is allowed.

keyTerms.meaning: Two תנאים (two teachers of the משנה era who disagree)
According to the opinion of the חכמים

steps.confusionAlert: The two תנאים are not arguing about the halacha itself. They disagree about what the חכמים actually said: whether the חכמים allow a smaller animal or not.

phrases.english: There are two תנאים,
phrases.notes: One is the תנא of our משנה and the other is the תנא of this ברייתא.

phrases.english: and they disagree about the opinion of the Rabbis.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting sources: two תנאים report the opinion of the חכמים differently.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and ברייתא both reflect one view of the חכמים, so the ברייתא's 'two rams' contradicts the משנה.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא's תנא holds the חכמים do not allow small for large, so he requires two rams. The משנה's תנא holds they do allow it.

steps.title: Reading an implication from רבי's reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי's reason again and infers that if mixing were possible, רבי would allow it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי forbids it because there is no mixing. The reason is only that there is no mixing; this implies that if there were mixing, it would be allowed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רבי's words in the ברייתא and draws a careful inference from them. This is setting up the גמרא's next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By saying his only reason is 'no mixing,' רבי seems to allow switching a bull for rams if mixing were possible. That is surprising, because step 7 showed רבי forbids switching even to a bigger animal. The גמרא is preparing to deal with this tension.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason (the only reason given)
But this implies (introduces the flip side of a statement)
It is permitted

phrases.english: רבי forbids it, because there is no mixing;
the reason is that there is no mixing,
but if there were mixing, it would be permitted.

steps.triggerLanguage: טַעְמָא דְּאֵין בִּילָּה, הָא יֵשׁ בִּילָּה שְׁרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא of step 9 to infer something new about רבי's view.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: From רבי's stated reason it follows that, if mixing were possible, he would allow buying two rams with the bull's money.

steps.title: A משנה where רבי forbids a simple swap of ram and lamb
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא cites a משנה in which רבי forbids using a blemished ram's money for a lamb, or a lamb's money for a ram. This suggests he objects to any change at all, not only to mixing.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in the משנה: if someone said 'This ram is an עולה' and it became blemished, he may use its money to bring a lamb if he wants. If he said 'This lamb is an עולה' and it became blemished, he may use its money to bring a ram. And רבי forbids it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges what it just inferred in Step 12, that רבי would allow switching if mixing were possible. It brings a משנה where רבי forbids a plain one-for-one switch.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 12 the גמרא said רבי's only reason is that there is 'no mixing.' But in this משנה, one ram is simply exchanged for one lamb, or one lamb for one ram, and רבי still forbids it. That makes it look as if רבי forbids any change from the original animal, even with no mixing problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Became blemished (unfit for the altar)
With its money, the money received when the blemished animal is redeemed
A ram (an older male sheep)
A lamb (a young male sheep)
Forbids

phrases.english: But didn't we learn in the mishna:
'This ram is a burnt offering,' and it became blemished,
if he wishes, he may bring a lamb with its money.
'This lamb is a burnt offering,' and it became blemished,
he may bring a ram with its money,
and Rabbi forbids it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference of Step 12 about רבי's reason.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that רבי forbids switching only because there is no mixing.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the משנה, רבי forbids a simple one-animal switch where mixing plays no role. So his objection seems to cover any change at all.

steps.title: Two תנאים disagree about רבי's view
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that two תנאים report רבי's opinion differently. In the ברייתא's version, רבי objects only because of mixing. In the משנה's version, רבי forbids any change.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are two תנאים, and they disagree about what רבי holds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by saying the ברייתא and the משנה are two different reports of רבי's opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is no need to make the two sources agree. The ברייתא's תנא holds that רבי forbids a switch only when there is no way to mix, so it would be allowed if mixing worked. The משנה's תנא holds that רבי forbids any change at all from the animal that was set aside, even a ram for a lamb.

keyTerms.meaning: Two תנאים (who hold different positions)
According to, in the view of

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same kind of answer as Step 11, but there the disagreement was about the חכמים. Here the disagreement is about רבי.

phrases.english: These are two tanna'im, and they disagree about the view of Rabbi.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge of Step 13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Two תנאים report רבי's opinion differently.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and the ברייתא give one and the same view of רבי, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא's version of רבי objects only because of mixing. The משנה's version of רבי forbids any change.

steps.title: With unblemished animals, bringing a bigger animal counts, following the חכמים
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא ends by ruling that if someone vowed a calf and brought a bull, or vowed a lamb and brought a ram, he has fulfilled his vow. The גמרא notes that this unnamed ruling follows the חכמים.
steps.simpleTranslation: And with unblemished animals: if he vowed a calf and brought a bull, or vowed a lamb and brought a ram, he has fulfilled his obligation. This unattributed ruling follows the חכמים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the last line of the ברייתא, which deals with animals that never became blemished, and tells us whose opinion it follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the animal was not blemished. The person simply brought a larger, more mature animal of the same kind than the one he promised, and it counts. Since this line has no name attached, the גמרא tells us it follows the חכמים; רבי would not agree.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: unblemished animals, fit for the altar
A calf (a young bull)
He has fulfilled his obligation
An unattributed ruling, stated with no name

phrases.english: And with unblemished animals,
phrases.notes: Literally 'pure ones.' Here it means animals that did not get a blemish, unlike all the cases before this.

phrases.english: if he vowed 'a calf' and brought a bull,
or vowed 'a lamb' and brought a ram, he has fulfilled his obligation.
This unattributed ruling follows the Rabbis.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes going through the ברייתא from Step 9 by explaining its last line.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With unblemished animals, bringing the bigger animal of the same kind fulfills the vow. This follows the חכמים, not רבי.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא's closing ruling on unblemished animals follows the חכמים. רבי disagrees with it.

steps.title: רב limits the rule of buying two bulls
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's rule that the money of a blemished bull can buy two bulls. רב says this applies only if the person said 'This bull is an עולה.' If he said 'This bull is upon me as an עולה,' his obligation is fixed.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: if he wishes, he may bring two with its money. רב מנשיא בר זביד said in the name of רב: they taught this only when he said 'This bull is an עולה.' But if he said 'This bull is upon me as an עולה,' his obligation is fixed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic. It quotes a line from the משנה and brings רב's limit on when that rule applies.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two wordings differ. 'This bull is an עולה' makes only that animal holy. 'Upon me' also makes the person himself responsible. In the second case his duty is fixed, so after the bull is blemished he must use its money to bring one bull, not split it into two.

keyTerms.meaning: They taught this only (in a certain case), a phrase that limits a rule
'This bull is an עולה': only the animal is made holy
'Upon me': the person takes on a personal obligation
It is fixed. His obligation is set and cannot be changed.

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the exact words of a vow change the law. Making an animal holy is different from taking on a personal obligation.

phrases.english: 'If he wishes, he may bring two with its money,' etc.
phrases.notes: This quotes the משנה about a blemished bull. The bracketed 'etc.' means 'and so on.'

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב מְנַשְּׁיָא בַּר זְבִיד אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Menashya bar Zevid said that Rav said:
They taught this only
where he said 'This bull is a burnt offering,'
but if he said 'This bull is upon me as a burnt offering,'
it is fixed.
phrases.notes: He means the obligation to bring one bull is locked in, so he can't use the money for two.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new line of the משנה and limits its rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה's permission to buy two bulls with the money of a blemished one applies only to 'This bull is an עולה.' With 'upon me,' the obligation is fixed and he must bring one bull.

steps.title: Maybe 'upon me' only means 'I will bring this one'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב's claim that saying 'This bull is upon me as an עולה' fixes the person's obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: But perhaps when he said 'upon me,' he only meant 'it is upon me to bring it'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב's rule from the last step. It suggests that the word 'עלי' may not mean what רב thought it meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said that adding 'עלי' turns the statement into a personal debt, so the owner stays responsible if the bull gets a blemish. The challenge: 'עלי' could simply mean 'I am responsible to bring this specific bull,' with no promise to replace it. If so, 'עלי' adds no extra responsibility, and רב's distinction falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: But perhaps (introduces another possible reading)
It is upon me to bring it (this specific animal only)
He is saying / he meant

phrases.english: But perhaps he is saying 'It is upon me to bring it'?
phrases.notes: He means he only promised to bring this bull, not to cover it if something happens to it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly challenges רב's distinction from Step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's claim that 'שור זה עלי עולה' fixes the owner's responsibility
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'עלי' may only mean a duty to bring this particular animal, not a guarantee to replace it, so it does not create a fixed obligation.

steps.title: רב's rule stated in a revised form
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא restates רב's rule: both 'This bull is an עולה' and 'This bull is upon me as an עולה' allow buying two bulls. Only 'This bull and its value are upon me' fixes the obligation.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if רב said something, this is what he said. רב מנשיא בר זביד said in the name of רב: The משנה only taught this when the person said 'This bull is an עולה' or 'This bull is upon me as an עולה.' But if he said 'This bull and its value are upon me as an עולה,' his obligation is fixed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts the challenge and corrects the record of what רב actually said. 'Upon me' alone is no longer enough to fix the obligation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge showed that 'עלי' alone might only mean 'I will bring this one.' So in this version 'עלי' is treated just like 'This bull is an עולה,' and the money may buy two bulls. Only when he adds 'ודמיו' (and its value) has he clearly taken on the bull's full worth, and then his obligation is fixed to one bull.

keyTerms.meaning: If it was said, this is how it was said (a corrected version of a teaching)
They only taught this in the case of
Or also
And its value (its money's worth)
It became fixed (the obligation is set)

steps.whatToRemember: Final version of רב: 'This bull is an עולה' and 'This bull is upon me as an עולה' are treated the same. Only 'This bull and its value are upon me' fixes the obligation.

phrases.english: Rather, if it was stated, it was stated like this:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב מְנַשְּׁיָא בַּר זְבִיד אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Menashya bar Zevid said that Rav said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא דְּאָמַר ״שׁוֹר זֶה עוֹלָה״,
phrases.english: They taught this only where he said 'This bull is a burnt offering,'
phrases.notes: 'This' means the משנה's rule that a blemished bull's money can buy two bulls.

phrases.aramaic: אִי נָמֵי אָמַר ״שׁוֹר זֶה עָלַי עוֹלָה״,
phrases.english: or also if he said 'This bull is upon me as a burnt offering,'

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אָמַר ״שׁוֹר זֶה וְדָמָיו עָלַי עוֹלָה״ –
phrases.english: but if he said 'This bull and its value are upon me as a burnt offering' –
it is fixed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the challenge of Step 17 and replaces רב's original wording with a revised version.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-stating the teacher's words (a corrected version of רב's statement)
steps.terutzMaskana: Only 'שור זה ודמיו עלי עולה' fixes the obligation; 'עלי' alone is like 'שור זה עולה'

steps.title: משנה: which animal is holy when one says 'one of my animals'
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: someone who consecrates 'one of my lambs/bulls' gives the larger of two or the middle of three. If he forgot which one he meant, the largest is holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who says 'One of my lambs is הקדש' or 'One of my bulls is הקדש,' and he has two, the larger of them is holy. If he has three, the middle one is holy. If he says 'I named one, but I don't know which,' or 'My father told me, but I don't know which,' the largest of them is holy.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It deals with someone who consecrates an animal without saying which one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three cases. With two animals, the larger is holy. With three, the middle one is holy. If he once named a specific animal and forgot which, or his father told him and he forgot, the largest is holy, because it might be the one that was meant.

keyTerms.meaning: משנה (marks the start of a new משנה)
Consecrated / holy property belonging to the Temple
The middle one (middle-sized)
I specified (I named which one)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the last case with the first two. In the first two cases he never picked an animal. In the last case he did pick one but forgot which, so the largest is holy.

phrases.english: MISHNAH: One who says 'One of my lambs is consecrated'
or 'One of my bulls is consecrated,'
and he had two –
the larger of them is consecrated.
Three – the middle one of them is consecrated.
'I specified, but I don't know what I specified,'

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ שֶׁ״אָמַר לִי אַבָּא, וְאֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ מַה״ –
phrases.english: or 'My father told me, but I don't know which' –
the largest of them is consecrated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic after the discussion of רב's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With two animals, the larger is holy. With three, the middle one is holy. If he specified one and forgot which, the largest is holy.

steps.title: Generous or stingy? The two cases seem to clash
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that the first case suggests a person consecrates generously, while the second case suggests he consecrates sparingly.
steps.simpleTranslation: It seems that one who consecrates does so generously. But look at the next case: the middle one is holy. It seems that one who consecrates does so sparingly!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts analyzing the משנה by pointing out a contradiction between its first two cases. The answer will come in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With two animals the larger one is holy, which suggests people give generously (עין יפה). But with three animals, if people were generous the largest would be holy. Making the middle one holy suggests people give sparingly (עין רעה). The same person cannot be both, so the משנה seems to contradict itself.

keyTerms.meaning: גמרא (marks the start of the גמרא's discussion)
Apparently / this shows that
A generous eye (giving generously)
A stingy eye (giving sparingly)
The latter clause of the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: Apparently, one who consecrates –
consecrates with a generous eye,
Say the latter clause:
The middle one of them is consecrated,
apparently, one who consecrates –
consecrates with a stingy eye!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַלְמָא מַקְדִּישׁ בְּעַיִן יָפָה מַקְדִּישׁ אֵימָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Analyzes the משנה just quoted and finds an apparent contradiction between its first two cases.
steps.kashyaTarget: The internal consistency of the משנה's first two cases
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first case implies people consecrate generously (larger animal). The second case implies they consecrate sparingly (middle, not largest). Both cannot be true.

steps.title: שמואל: we also worry about the middle animal
steps.stepSummary: שמואל explains that the person always consecrates generously. In the case of three animals, the largest is holy, and we must also worry that the middle one is holy, since next to the small one it is a generous choice.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: We are also concerned about the middle animal, because compared to the small one, giving the middle one is generous.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל answers the contradiction from Step 20 by showing that both cases of the משנה follow the same idea: a person consecrates generously.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's words 'the middle of three' do not mean that only the middle one is holy. The largest is surely holy, and the middle one also might be, because choosing it over the smallest still counts as generous. So there is no 'sparing' approach anywhere in the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: We are concerned, we must take into account the possibility
The middle one (here, the middle-sized animal)
A generous eye, giving generously
The small one

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read the משנה as saying the middle animal is holy instead of the largest. According to שמואל, the largest is holy, and the middle one is only a possible addition.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:
We are concerned also about the middle one,
for compared to the small one, it is a generous choice.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the contradiction raised in Step 20 between the two cases of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the משנה's second case so that it matches the first
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The middle-of-three ruling seemed to show that a person consecrates sparingly.
steps.terutzMaskana: The largest is holy, and the middle one is a possible additional holy animal, because it is still generous compared to the smallest.

steps.title: What should the owner actually do?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the owner should handle the situation, since only one animal is really holy but it is unclear which.
steps.simpleTranslation: How should he act?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical question and sets up the next step, which gives the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After שמואל, both the largest and the middle animal might be the holy one. But the person only consecrated one animal, so the גמרא wants to know how to bring the right one to the מזבח.

keyTerms.meaning: How does he act? What should he do?

phrases.english: How should he act?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows from שמואל's ruling, which leaves two animals in doubt.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical procedure for dealing with the doubt between the largest and the middle animal.

steps.title: Wait for a blemish and move the holiness to the large animal
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר רב says the owner waits until the middle animal gets a blemish, then transfers its holiness onto the large animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר רב said: He waits until it becomes blemished, and then transfers its holiness onto the large animal.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא בר רב answers the practical question from Step 22.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An unblemished holy animal cannot just be released from its holiness. So the owner waits until the middle animal gets a blemish, then moves its possible holiness onto the large animal. Now the large animal is holy either way and can be brought as the קרבן.

keyTerms.meaning: Becomes blemished (from מוּם)
Transfers away, releases the holiness
Holiness

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Rav said:
He waits for it until it becomes blemished,
and transfers its holiness onto the large one.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר רַב: מַמְתִּין לוֹ עַד שֶׁיּוּמַם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Wait until the middle animal is blemished, then transfer its holiness onto the large animal.

steps.title: 'A bull among my bulls' means the largest
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן, quoting רבה בר אבוה, says the משנה's ruling about the middle animal applies only when the person said 'One of my bulls is consecrated.' If he said 'A bull among my bulls is consecrated,' only the largest is holy.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said in the name of רבה בר אבוה: They taught this only when he said 'One of my bulls is consecrated.' But if he said 'A bull among my bulls is consecrated,' the largest of them is holy, because he means 'the bull among my bulls.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה and adds a limit: the exact wording of the vow decides which animal becomes holy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'One of my bulls' is open, so the middle one might also count. But 'a bull among my bulls' sounds like 'the bull,' the standout one in the herd. So that wording points only to the largest.

keyTerms.meaning: They taught this only in a case where... (limits a ruling)
Consecrated, belonging to the בית המקדש
A bull among my bulls
'The bull among my bulls,' meaning the outstanding one

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that small changes in the wording of a vow can change which animal becomes holy.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן, אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ:
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said that Rabba bar Avuh said:
They taught this only when he said:
phrases.notes: This goes back to the משנה in Step 19, which says the middle of three is holy.

phrases.english: 'One of my bulls is consecrated.'
But if he said 'A bull among my bulls is consecrated' –
the largest of them is consecrated,
since he is saying 'the bull among my bulls.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן, אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר אֲבוּהּ: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new discussion that limits the משנה's ruling according to the wording used.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'One of my bulls' follows the משנה's rule. 'A bull among my bulls' makes only the largest holy.

steps.title: Challenge from עולא's case of selling a house
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבה בר אבוה from עולא's ruling: someone who sells 'a house among my houses' may show the buyer a loft. That seems to be because 'a house among my houses' points to the worst one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רב הונא said in the name of רבי חייא, quoting עולא: If someone tells his friend 'I am selling you a house among my houses,' he may show him a loft. Isn't that because it is the worst?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the claim of Step 24 with a case that uses the same kind of wording but seems to point to the lowest-quality item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה בר אבוה read 'X among my X's' as the best one. עולא's case uses the same wording, 'a house among my houses,' and lets the seller give a loft, which seems to be the worst house. That suggests 'a bull among my bulls' should mean the smallest bull, not the largest.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? (opens a challenge)
A house among my houses
A loft, an upstairs room
Inferior, worse

phrases.english: Is that so? But didn't Rav Huna say
that Rabbi Ḥiyya said in the name of Ulla:
One who says to his friend:
'I am selling you a house among my houses' –
may show him a loft.
Is it not because it is the worst?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reading of 'a bull among my bulls' from Step 24.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר אבוה's claim that 'a bull among my bulls' means the largest bull.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In עולא's case the same kind of wording lets the seller give the worst house, so the same wording for bulls should mean the worst bull.

steps.title: No, it means the best of the houses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that עולא's ruling also refers to the best of the houses, so it agrees with רבה בר אבוה.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, it means the best of the houses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the reading of עולא's ruling that the challenge relied on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumed that 'a house among my houses' points to the worst house. The answer says it actually points to the best one. So both cases follow the same rule: 'X among my X's' means the top one, and רבה בר אבוה's ruling stands.

keyTerms.meaning: The best, the most excellent

steps.whatToRemember: 'One of my animals' allows the middle of three to be possibly holy, alongside the largest. 'An animal among my animals' means only the best, and עולא's house case is explained the same way.

phrases.english: No, the best of the houses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 25.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: עולא's case meant the seller gives the worst house.
steps.terutzMaskana: עולא's case refers to the best of the houses, which matches רבה בר אבוה.

steps.title: A ברייתא seems to treat all the bulls as doubtful
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבה בר אבוה from a ברייתא. In the case of 'a bull among my bulls is holy' the ברייתא says the largest is holy, but it also says all the bulls must be sold for עולות. That suggests every bull is in doubt.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: 'A bull among my bulls is holy,' and likewise a holy bull that got mixed with others: the largest of them is holy, and all of them are sold for the needs of burnt offerings, and the money paid for them is not holy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to attack רבה בר אבוה's rule that 'a bull among my bulls' makes only the largest holy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says all the bulls must be sold to people who need עולות. You would only do that if each bull might be the holy one. So it seems that saying 'a bull among my bulls' leaves every bull in doubt, not just the largest.

keyTerms.meaning: A bull among my bulls
Got mixed up with
For the needs of burnt offerings (sold to people who must bring an עולה)
And the money paid for them is not holy

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא does say 'the largest is holy,' which sounds like רבה בר אבוה. The problem is the next line: if only the largest were holy, why would all the others need to be sold for עולות?

phrases.english: They challenged: 'A bull among my bulls is holy,'
and likewise a holy bull
that got mixed with other bulls:
the largest of them is holy,
and all of them are sold for the needs of burnt offerings,
and the money paid for them is not holy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defending רבה בר אבוה against עולא's ruling, the גמרא brings a new challenge from a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר אבוה's rule that 'a bull among my bulls' makes only the largest holy (Step 24).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא requires all the bulls to be sold for עולות, which shows every bull is treated as possibly holy.

steps.title: The doubt about all the bulls is only in the mixed-up case
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ruling 'all are sold for עולות' refers only to the second case, a holy bull that got mixed with others.
steps.simpleTranslation: Explain it as referring to a holy bull that got mixed with others.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by saying the 'sell them all' ruling only applies to the mixed-up bull case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a holy bull got mixed in, nobody knows which one it was, so every bull is in doubt. But when a person says 'a bull among my bulls,' he meant the largest, so there is no doubt. רבה בר אבוה's rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Explain it as (read the ruling as referring to)

phrases.english: Explain it as referring to a holy bull
that got mixed with others.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting part of the ברייתא to one of its two cases.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ruling that all bulls are sold for עולות applies to both cases in the ברייתא.
steps.terutzMaskana: That ruling applies only to the case of a holy bull mixed with others.

steps.title: But the ברייתא says 'and similarly'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: the ברייתא joined the two cases with 'וכן' ('and similarly'), so the same rulings should apply to both.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it says 'and similarly'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer it just gave, pointing to the word 'וכן' in the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'וכן' links the two cases together. That suggests everything said after it, including 'all are sold for עולות,' applies to 'a bull among my bulls' too.

keyTerms.meaning: But look, ... (introduces a push-back)
And similarly (links two cases to one ruling)

phrases.english: But it says 'and similarly'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that 'all are sold' refers only to the mixed-up case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'וכן' puts both cases under the same rulings.

steps.title: 'Similarly' only refers to the largest being holy
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that 'similarly' applies only to the ruling that the largest bull is holy, which is true in both cases.
steps.simpleTranslation: Explain it as referring to the largest.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word 'וכן' connects the two cases only for the ruling 'the largest is holy.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both cases share one ruling: the largest bull is holy. The extra ruling, that all the bulls are sold for עולות, belongs only to the mixed-up case. So the ברייתא fits רבה בר אבוה.

keyTerms.meaning: The largest one

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא is read in two layers: 'the largest is holy' applies to both cases, but 'all are sold for עולות' applies only when a holy bull got mixed up.

phrases.english: Explain it as referring to the largest.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the reach of the linking word 'וכן'.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'וכן' makes every ruling apply to both cases.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'וכן' only shares the ruling that the largest is holy.

steps.title: Selling 'a house among my houses' lets him give the fallen one
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another ברייתא: someone who sells 'a house among my houses' can hand over a house that fell down, and someone who sells 'a slave among my slaves' can hand over one who died. This seems to show the wording does not point to the best one.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: 'I am selling you a house among my houses,' and one fell down: he may show him the fallen one. 'I am selling you a slave among my slaves,' and one died: he may show him the dead one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to challenge רבה בר אבוה. The answer comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'a house among my houses' meant the best house, the seller could not hand over a ruined one. Since he can give the fallen house or the dead slave, it seems this wording does not point to the best, which goes against רבה בר אבוה.

keyTerms.meaning: A house among my houses
He shows him (he points to it as the one sold)
Fallen, collapsed

phrases.english: They challenged: 'I am selling you a house among my houses,'
and one fell down: he may show him the fallen one,
phrases.notes: He can say 'this is the house I sold you,' so the buyer takes the loss.

phrases.english: 'I am selling you a slave among my slaves,'
and one died: he may show him the dead one.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After resolving the bull ברייתא, the גמרא opens a new challenge from a sales ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה בר אבוה's rule that 'X among my X' points to the best one (Step 24), and the reading of עולא in Step 26.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The seller may give the fallen house or dead slave, so this wording does not point to the best.
